title: A Reproducible Synthetic Benchmark and Deterministic Validator for Evaluating LLM‑Driven NetOps: A Paired Confirmatory Comparison of a GVR Pipeline and Single‑Pass Generation
abstract: We designed, preregistered, and executed a sealed, machine‑checkable synthetic benchmark and deterministic validator to compare a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline against a frozen single‑pass LLM on operational intent→configuration tasks. The preregistered paired design used N=300 tasks (four intent clusters, 75 tasks each) and declared model gpt-5-mini; validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0). The experiment used a shared‑initial generation: baseline and guarded conditions received the same generated candidate; the guarded pipeline invoked repair only upon validator failure and was limited to one repair call per task. Provider accounting shows 300 shared initial generation calls and exactly one repair invocation (model_calls_used = 301). Results: baseline 299/300 passes, guarded 300/300 passes; contingency n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; paired difference = 0.0033333333333332993; paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The preregistered hypothesis that GVR produces a materially higher pass rate (target effect 0.10 at ≈80% power with N=300) was not supported. We diagnose causes (ceiling effect; minimal GVR engagement), present complete execution accounting and reproducibility pointers (notably execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d and execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820), and provide artifact‑grounded benchmark design recommendations. All preregistration, per‑task validator traces, provider traces, and analysis artifacts are archived for community reuse.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are proposed for NetOps tasks including intent→configuration translation, change planning, and automated remediation. Prior work shows that LLMs can draft device configurations but may produce syntax, topology, or semantic errors unless paired with verification and human oversight. Community need: standardized, machine‑checkable benchmarks that couple operational intent tasks with deterministic validator semantics and sealed preregistration to support confirmatory comparisons of defended pipelines (generate–validate–repair, GVR) versus single‑pass generation. To address this, we preregistered and executed study ac-2026-003-prereg-v1: a sealed paired experiment comparing a guarded GVR pipeline against a single‑pass LLM (declared gpt-5-mini) on N=300 synthetic intent→configuration tasks. The experiment used a shared‑initial generation design so that baseline and guarded conditions used the same initial candidate for each task; the guarded pipeline could invoke at most one automated repair per task, only when the deterministic validator failed. Our primary confirmatory question: under fixed seeds and this constrained repair budget, does GVR materially increase the per‑task validator pass rate relative to a frozen single‑pass LLM?
sections.related_work: Recent surveys and focused studies document rapid growth in LLM applications to network operations and summarize open evaluation and safety gaps. Work on intent→configuration translation and verifier‑assisted prompting reports that generate–validate–repair or verifier‑guided repair can reduce misconfigurations in specific settings, though often with human oversight and limited task scope. Security and robustness research documents prompt injection, jailbreaks, and hallucination risks relevant to operational automation, motivating conservative validator designs. These prior findings motivate building reproducible, artifact‑grounded benchmarks with deterministic validators to isolate repair efficacy and to quantify operational risk and benefit under sealed experimental protocols [W4406137434, W4415071524, W4402742293, W4404652946].
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary hypothesis. We preregistered study ac-2026-003-prereg-v1 prior to execution. Primary H1: the GVR pipeline yields a higher per‑task validator pass rate than a frozen single‑pass generator on N=300 paired tasks (two‑sided α=0.05). The preregistration specified task composition, validator semantics, adapter and model settings, sampling and repair budgets, exclusion rules, missingness treatments, and the analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1).

Task bank and semantics. A deterministic task generator produced N=300 synthetic intent→configuration tasks partitioned into four intent clusters (reachability, isolation, ACLs, route policies; 75 tasks each). Each task encodes initial_state, expected_final_state, allowed_fields, workflow_policies, and an explicit required_sequence that defines the intended safe sequence of field changes. Tasks cover device counts 3–50 and abstract multi‑vendor device models; they contain no private customer data and are synthetic by design.

Deterministic validator. deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version v5.0) implements full_intent_constraint_validation. The validator applies snapshot semantics: it parses the candidate configuration, checks required command sequences, workflow_policies (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields, final_group_constraints), and expected_final_state; it deterministically returns VALID_CONFIGURATION or enumerated violation codes. This conservative, stateless validator produces binary pass/fail outcomes suitable for confirmatory inference.

Shared‑initial paired design and repair budget. To tightly control generator variance the pipeline generated a single shared initial candidate per task (shared_initial_generation stage). That shared candidate served as the baseline single‑pass output. For the guarded condition the validator evaluated the same shared candidate, and only if the validator failed was the repair stage permitted up to one automated repair call (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). The preregistered planned_episode_count = 600 (300 shared initial + up to 300 repairs). This design ensures improvement under guarded must arise from repair acting on the same initial candidate rather than from multiple independent generations.

Model and adapter configuration. The hosted adapter used declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini" (requested_model = "gpt-5-mini") with max_output_tokens = 2000, maximum_attempts_per_call = 1, reasoning_effort = "minimal", store = false, and temperature unset; the adapter operated in a deterministic sampling mode (see Reproducibility section). Model and runtime artifacts are archived (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820).

Exclusions, missingness, and analysis plan. Exclusion rules removed items matching private‑data regexes or ambiguous specifications; none occurred in the final run. Missingness plan required ≥270 completed pairs; the run completed 300. The primary estimand was paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline on N=300 paired binary outcomes; the preregistered test was exact McNemar two‑sided. A paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI was computed with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). Sensitivity analyses (registered) treated missing/failed calls as failures; no such events occurred.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and provider audit. Execution completed per preregistration: planned_episode_count = 600, completed_episode_count = 600, complete_pair_count = 300, failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 301. Provider_call_audit recorded stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1} and condition_counts = {shared: 300, guarded: 1}; therefore the guarded repair stage executed exactly once under the preregistered repair budget. Authoritative raw results and per‑call provider traces are archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d) and execution/task_manifest.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 062b80216e49a2919ebf8debd75cf02fffcfd752b5b253e5a11c0701ca853097).

Primary confirmatory outcomes. Aggregated counts: baseline_success_count = 299/300 (baseline_success_rate = 0.9966666666666667); guarded_success_count = 300/300 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). Paired contingency (guarded vs baseline): n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0033333333333332993. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI (percentile, 10,000 resamples, seed 1729): [0.00, 0.01]. Table 1 summarizes these counts and statistics.

Representative per‑task diagnostics. The archived scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/*.json) provide deterministic validator traces for every task: normalized_configuration, required_command_count, parsed_command_count, final_state, and violation lists when present. Representative examples (task-000001 … task-000006) illustrate multi‑step required sequences (e.g., shutdown_configure_restore, make_before_break_uplink_switchover, paired_link_atomic_mtu_change) and show identical shared candidate content across baseline and guarded conditions for most tasks. For tasks in the archive, shared_initial candidate SHA‑256 values and per‑call provider traces are included (example: task-000001 shared_initial_provider_trace_sha256 = 97c4832c5575d069ff608f7e5c9116d3428e8ca4a5e20ce5d8625c395900121a).

Discordant pair and repair trace archival. The run produced a single discordant pair (n10=1: guarded passed, baseline failed) and a single repair invocation. The single repair provider trace and the complete identifier for the discordant episode are contained in the authoritative raw results and provider traces file execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d) and are indexed in the execution manifest. Reproducers and auditors should extract that artifact (execution/raw_results.jsonl) to obtain the exact pair identifier and the repair provider trace; the execution manifest and analysis artifacts include full hashes and file indices to verify extraction integrity.

Post‑hoc power and sensitivity arithmetic. The preregistered power calculation targeted detection of a 0.10 absolute paired improvement at ≈80% power with N=300 under conservative discordance assumptions. The observed baseline ≈0.997 violates those assumptions: arithmetic shows that, given baseline success 299/300, the maximum possible absolute paired improvement is 1/300 ≈ 0.00333, far smaller than the preregistered target. This direct arithmetic explains the null confirmatory outcome and is reported precisely in the archived analysis artifacts.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation: ceiling effect and constrained repair engagement. The preregistered hypothesis was not supported because (1) the shared_initial generator produced near‑perfect candidates (baseline 299/300), leaving almost no headroom for the preregistered detectable effect, and (2) the guarded policy invoked repair only on validator failures and the validator accepted 299 of 300 shared candidates, causing the repair subsystem to execute only once. Consequently, the paired test compared identical shared candidates in 299 pairs and only one pair differed — insufficient for statistical rejection.

Operational implications. These results do not imply that GVR pipelines are universally unhelpful. Rather, they show that under a shared‑initial, single‑repair budget and with a generator that is highly successful on the chosen synthetic tasks, repair has limited opportunity to contribute. Operationally, when generator accuracy is already near ceiling on a task distribution, resources may be better directed to (a) improving generator diversity measurements, (b) designing harder or adversarial task distributions, or (c) allowing multi‑attempt or stateful repair policies that can iterate beyond a single repair call.

Concrete benchmark design recommendations (artifact‑grounded). From execution accounting and per‑task validator diagnostics we recommend: (A) increase task difficulty or introduce adversarial seeds to raise initial failure rates; (B) allow iterative repair budgets (multiple repair attempts per failed candidate) so repair can act progressively; (C) evaluate multiple independent generation samples per task (instead of a shared‑initial design) to measure generator variance and selection effects; (D) extend validators toward stateful or temporal emulation to capture in‑flight side effects and ordering constraints rather than snapshot checks. Each recommendation follows directly from recorded facts: 300 shared initial generations, exactly 1 repair invocation, and validator diagnostics archived per task.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: prompt and adapter sensitivity (deterministic sampling) can affect shared‑initial outputs; we preserved adapter and prompt artifacts (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = a40e96e2...) and the immutable initial master prompt reference (provenance/master_prompt.txt SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1...) to enable controlled reproduction. Construct validity: the validator uses snapshot semantics and may not capture vendor CLI idiosyncrasies or asynchronous side effects. External validity: tasks are synthetic and abstract multi‑vendor models; only the declared model gpt-5-mini was evaluated. Conclusion validity: the ceiling effect reduced inferential power for the preregistered target; the paired design remains correct but underpowered given observed margins.

Reproducibility guidance. Deterministic reproduction requires: (1) access to the same hosted model release and provider invocation semantics recorded in execution/model_configuration.json (SHA‑256 = a40e96e212ab87da...); (2) replay or inspection of per‑call provider traces archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29...); (3) use of the archived task manifest (execution/task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 = 062b8021...) and scoring artifacts (execution/scoring/*.json). The raw results file contains the single repair provider trace and the exact identifier for the single discordant pair; auditors should extract those entries for item‑level inspection.

Limitations and future work. Primary limits: snapshot validator semantics, synthetic task scope, single declared model, and a constrained single‑repair budget that prevented broad assessment of iterative repair efficacy. Future work should increase task difficulty, permit iterative repairs, evaluate multi‑generation baselines, and extend validators toward stateful emulation. The archived bundle enables these follow‑on studies without reconstructing our pipeline.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a sealed synthetic benchmark and deterministic validator and ran a paired confirmatory comparison of a guarded GVR pipeline versus a frozen single‑pass gpt-5-mini generator on N=300 intent→configuration tasks. Both approaches achieved near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300; guarded 300/300). The preregistered hypothesis that GVR materially improves pass rate (target 0.10) was not supported. Execution accounting shows the guarded repair stage executed only once across N=300 tasks; consequently the guarded condition rarely differed from baseline. We release the full preregistration, execution manifest, raw responses, per‑task validator traces, and analysis artifacts so the community can extend the benchmark with harder tasks, iterative repair budgets, and multi‑model comparisons to better evaluate when GVR pipelines provide measurable operational value.

limitations: Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces snapshot intent constraints but does not model temporal in‑flight execution dynamics, vendor CLI idiosyncrasies, or asynchronous side effects.

External validity: tasks are synthetic (device counts 3–50, abstracted multi‑vendor models) and may not capture production heterogeneity; findings do not imply equivalent performance on real production networks or private customer data.

Ceiling effect: near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300, guarded 300/300) reduce sensitivity to detect the preregistered target effect (0.10) and therefore constrain confirmatory inference about practical superiority of GVR under broader conditions.
Model and scope limits: only gpt-5-mini was declared and evaluated; findings do not generalize to other model families or sizes without further experiments.

GVR engagement: the guarded repair stage executed only once across N=300 tasks (provider recorded stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 300, repair = 1), so the guarded condition rarely differed from baseline; this pipeline inactivity constrains conclusions about repair effectiveness under alternative trigger policies or larger repair budgets.
Failure‑mode analysis: only one discordant outcome occurred (n10=1), leaving exploratory failure clustering and subgroup inference underpowered and inconclusive.

Reproducibility caveat: reproducing identical hosted model outputs may require access to the same hosted model release and provider invocation semantics recorded in execution/model_configuration.json and the per‑call provider traces archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl.

Artifact‑inclusion note: the exact per‑task artifacts that contain the single repair provider trace and the single discordant episode identifier are present in the archived execution bundle (execution manifest and raw_results) and are authoritative for auditors.
